clue.text: Perhaps King is rejected; likewise, the odd bits of Pullman novel

indicators.note: rejected means turned back, so the word for the king is read backwards

parts.note: a king is one example of a playing card, hence the 'Perhaps'

indicators.note: 'likewise' carries 'rejected' on to the odd bits, so those are thrown away and the even letters are kept
the odd-numbered letters of the following word are the ones in question here

explanation.surface: A literary put-down: Stephen King's book is turned down, and so are scraps of a Philip Pullman novel.
explanation.walkthrough: King looks like Stephen King but is a playing card. 'likewise' carries 'rejected' over to the odd letters of Pullman, so those go and the even ones stay.
explanation.definitionFit: Bram Stoker's Dracula is a Gothic novel of 1897, named for its vampire count.

clue.text: Novel about second wife being turned queen by dictating Boris?

indicators.note: turned means flipped round, so the queen's letters run backwards

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the usual abbreviation for the Queen

indicators.note: dictating is speaking words to be written down, so the surname is taken as it is spoken

parts.note: Boris Becker, the German tennis champion

explanation.surface: A fanciful image of a second wife being turned into a queen at Boris Johnson's dictation.
explanation.walkthrough: Boris looks like Johnson but is the tennis player Boris Becker; said in a British accent (no final R), BECKER sounds like BECCA.
explanation.definitionFit: Du Maurier's novel is narrated by the second Mrs de Winter, haunted by her predecessor.

clue.text: Substance ultimately covered by jam?

indicators.note: covered by means held within, so the last letter goes inside the other word

parts.note: to jam is to cram, to pack something in tight

indicators.note: ultimately means at the very end, so only the final letter of the word is used

explanation.surface: A cream tea riddle: which substance ends up underneath the jam?
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue describes the Devon way of serving a scone, jam spread over the cream; the question mark admits the Cornish do it the other way round.
explanation.definitionFit: On a Devon cream tea, clotted cream goes on the scone first and the jam on top of it.

clue.text: Fresher wants a little paperclip piercing

indicators.note: a little says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A university fresher fancies a modest body piercing made with a paperclip.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft took 'Fresher wants' as the definition, but LIPPIER means only fresher; 'wants' is a link word joining definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Fresh can mean cheeky or impudent, as can lippy, so the comparatives match.

clue.text: Salacious dancing leaving us out? That's not very friendly

indicators.note: dancing letters move about, so the word is rearranged
with 'out', leaving out says the two letters of 'us' are dropped from the mix
completes 'leaving ... out', taking the pair of letters away

explanation.surface: Someone excluded from a racy dance complains that this is rather unfriendly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dancing' rearranges SALACIOUS and 'leaving us out' removes U and S from the mix before the letters are reordered.
explanation.definitionFit: An asocial person avoids or is indifferent to company, so the word describes unfriendliness.

clue.text: Short novel acquired by agent

indicators.note: acquired by means taken into, so the novel's title goes inside the agent

parts.note: a secret agent is a spy
Kim is Rudyard Kipling's novel of the Great Game

explanation.surface: A short book bought up by a literary agent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short novel' reads as one phrase, a novella; 'Short' is the definition and 'novel' is Kipling's Kim.
explanation.definitionFit: Skimpy clothing or rations are scant, too small: in short supply.

clue.text: Short novel repeatedly describing love for women's footwear

indicators.note: to describe a circle is to draw round it, so the word goes around the zero

parts.note: short, as in abrupt in manner, is curt
love is nil in tennis scoring, the letter O

indicators.note: repeatedly says the same going-round of zero happens a second time, to the novel

parts.note: She is H. Rider Haggard's adventure novel

explanation.surface: A short romance that keeps describing love, sold as a ladies' shoe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short novel' tempts as a novella, but the two words give separate pieces; 'repeatedly' makes 'describing' wrap each of them round the love letter in turn.
explanation.definitionFit: A court shoe is a woman's plain low-cut shoe with no fastening, often with a heel.

clue.text: Opposing sides on Armstrong's cycling disgrace

indicators.note: the sides of a word are its outermost letters, first and last
cycling moves letters round from the front to the back of the word

parts.note: a stain on one's name is a disgrace

explanation.surface: Lance Armstrong's doping scandal is a disgrace to cycling, and everyone's against him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cycling' wants to be about Lance Armstrong's sport; here it moves ST from the front of STAIN to the back, giving AINST.
explanation.definitionFit: Against and opposing both mean set in opposition to something.

clue.text: Novel's pathetic protagonist losing ring but winning old cash

indicators.note: winning means taking in, so the mixed letters take the old money inside them
pathetic in its old sense is moving, and the letters are moved about
losing says a letter is taken away from the mixed word

parts.note: a ring is round, the letter O
tin is old slang for money

explanation.surface: A sad hero who loses a ring but wins some cash: the story of a novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pathetic' is an unusual anagram signal, from its old sense of moving. The rearranged letters, less one O, make TRAINSPOTG, and the old money sits inside before the G.
explanation.definitionFit: Trainspotting is Irvine Welsh's 1993 novel about heroin users in Edinburgh.

clue.text: Instrument with which old boy regularly trimmed novel

parts.note: OB is the abbreviation for old boy, a former pupil

indicators.note: regularly trimmed means every other letter is cut away, keeping the rest

explanation.surface: An old schoolboy trimmed a novel down with some instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: The oboe is a double-reed woodwind instrument of the orchestra.

clue.text: First section of novel copper initially labelled as rather peculiar

parts.note: a novel's first section is Part I
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so the first letter of each of the next three words is taken

explanation.surface: The opening of a novel features a policeman described as rather odd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'copper' looks like a police officer but is the element Cu.
explanation.definitionFit: Particular and peculiar both mean belonging to one case alone, as in 'peculiar to'.

clue.text: Defraud a character shipwrecked in novel for seafood

parts.note: to scam someone is to defraud them
Pi Patel is shipwrecked in Yann Martel's novel Life of Pi

explanation.surface: A conman cheats a castaway in a novel out of the seafood.
explanation.definitionFit: Scampi are langoustine tails, usually served breaded and fried.

clue.text: Independent parliamentarian to back hospital department without effect

parts.note: an MP is a Member of Parliament

indicators.note: back means reversed here, so the little word is read the other way

parts.note: ENT is the ear, nose and throat department

explanation.surface: An independent MP backs a hospital department, but achieves nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Impotent means powerless, unable to produce any result.

clue.text: Hotel to show former president embracing reading? One may go into shock …

parts.note: H is Hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet
to air something is to show it in public

indicators.note: embracing means holding inside, so the president's name wraps the letter

parts.note: Bush, either US president of that name
reading is one of the three Rs, so R

explanation.surface: A hotel puts on a former president reading something shocking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shock' sounds like trauma, but it is a shock of hair, a thick mop a brush is run through.
explanation.definitionFit: A hairbrush is pulled through a mass of hair, a shock being a bushy head of it.

clue.text: Endlessly greedy duck caught rowing team and coach again

indicators.note: endlessly means each word loses its first and last letters
caught as in heard: 'I caught what you said', so it is the spoken word

parts.note: a racing boat's crew of eight rowers is an eight

explanation.surface: A greedy duck keeps snatching bread while the rowing team's coach tries again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'caught' looks like cricket's C, but means heard: EIGHT spoken sounds like ATE. 'Endlessly' trims both greedy and duck, giving REED and UC.
explanation.definitionFit: To re-educate is to teach or train again, as a coach does.

clue.text: … Novel abandoned, he hit "Tweet"

indicators.note: abandoned, wild and unrestrained, signals the letters are thrown about

explanation.surface: Continuing from the hairbrush: someone gave up on a novel and sent a tweet.
explanation.definitionFit: White Teeth is Zadie Smith's debut novel of 2000, set in north London.

clue.text: Novel Methuselah's written about himself?

indicators.note: written about means set down around, so the pronoun wraps the other word

parts.note: the setter, Methuselah, would say 'my' of what is his
one is the impersonal self, as in 'one's self'

explanation.surface: The setter wonders aloud about writing an autobiographical novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Methuselah is this puzzle's setter, so 'Methuselah's' is the setter's MY.
explanation.definitionFit: Money: A Suicide Note is Martin Amis's 1984 novel.

clue.text: Modernist novel which introduces a certain Bloom

definitions.meaning: Virginia Woolf's ..., a modernist novel of 1928
... is the first name of the actor ... Bloom, so it comes before Bloom

explanation.surface: A modernist novel that brings in a character called Bloom, as Joyce did.
explanation.walkthrough: Bloom suggests Leopold Bloom of Joyce's Ulysses; it is the actor Orlando Bloom.
explanation.definitionFit: Woolf's Orlando is a modernist novel, and Orlando precedes the actor's surname Bloom.

clue.text: Informal academic and university fellows taking time with special papers

parts.note: doc is a casual name for a doctor, an academic title
fellows are men

explanation.surface: A casual don and some university fellows take time over special papers.
explanation.definitionFit: Documents are official papers, records written or printed.

clue.text: Doctor Seuss' extremely loopy novel

indicators.note: to doctor is to tamper with, so the letters are rearranged
extremely means at the extremes, the first and last letters

explanation.surface: Dr Seuss's wild children's books might be called an extremely loopy novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' reads as Dr Seuss's title, but is the anagram signal for SEUSS plus LY.
explanation.definitionFit: Ulysses is James Joyce's 1922 modernist novel set over one Dublin day.

clue.text: Royal starts to moan about libel after article produced by Heat

indicators.note: after puts the royal letters behind the article

parts.note: the is the definite article

indicators.note: starts to means the first letters of the next three words

explanation.surface: A royal begins complaining about a libel published in Heat, the celebrity magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: Heat is a British celebrity gossip magazine, hence the capital; the definition means produced by heat.
explanation.definitionFit: Thermal energy or currents are those caused by warmth.

clue.text: Very European city on the coast is novel's deadly location

parts.note: Nice is a city on the French Riviera coast

explanation.surface: A European coastal city is the setting for a novel's death.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deadly location' points to Thomas Mann's novella Death in Venice.
explanation.definitionFit: Death in Venice is set in that city, so it is where the novel's death happens.

clue.text: Possibly be artful as a novelist

indicators.note: possibly signals one possible arrangement of the letters

explanation.surface: Advice to aspiring writers: be artful, as a novelist should.
explanation.definitionFit: Gustave Flaubert was a French novelist, author of Madame Bovary.

clue.text: Talk of young affirming their truth enrages right-wing leaders

indicators.note: leaders are front letters, so the first letter of each of the six words is taken

parts.words: young affirming their truth enrages right-wing

explanation.surface: Young people speaking their truth infuriate right-wing figures.
explanation.definitionFit: To yatter is to chatter on at length, an informal word for idle talk.

clue.text: See 16
Where suits might be heard … or certain cases?

indicators.note: heard means the phrase is taken as it is spoken

parts.note: card suits are laid out in patience, the solo card game, so they are in patience

explanation.surface: Following on from the novel: where lawsuits can be heard, or perhaps some legal cases?
explanation.walkthrough: 'suits' suggests lawsuits and 'cases' legal ones; suits are card suits and cases are hospital cases. Patience is the British name for the card game solitaire.
explanation.definitionFit: Inpatients are hospital cases, patients who stay in overnight.

clue.text: Insiders made money in jazz age Fitzgerald novel

indicators.note: insiders are the inner letters, and made says they are turned into something else

parts.note: Ella Fitzgerald, the jazz singer
M is the abbreviation for money, here used for each of the two inner letters

explanation.surface: Insiders profited in the jazz age, as in a Fitzgerald novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jazz age Fitzgerald' suggests F. Scott but is the singer Ella; her two inner letters are each made M.
explanation.definitionFit: Emma is Jane Austen's 1815 novel about a meddling matchmaker.

clue.text: Comedian's debut novel after leaving the Fringe read aloud and reviewed?

indicators.note: after puts the trimmed novel behind the comedian's first letter
a debut is a first appearance, so the first letter is taken
the fringe of a word is its edge letters, so the outer ones are dropped
aloud means the word is taken as spoken, past tense

parts.note: read in the past tense is pronounced like the colour red

explanation.surface: A comedian's first novel, after the Edinburgh Fringe, read out and reviewed.
explanation.walkthrough: The Fringe is the Edinburgh festival where comedians perform; here it is the outer letters of novel. 'read' past tense sounds like RED.
explanation.definitionFit: A newspaper that covers an event reports on it, as a critic reviews a show.

clue.text: Pitch a second Plath novel

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters take a new order

explanation.surface: Pitching a second Sylvia Plath novel to a publisher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pitch' looks like a book pitch; it is the tarry substance, and 'novel' is an anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Pitch is the black tarry residue, and asphalt is a bitumen paving material of the same kind.
